query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles that are kinetically trapped in a high-entropy, disordered state during rapid low‐temperature synthesis preserve their single-phase structure and chemical homogeneity under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions, because the synthesis locks the constituent elements in place by severely limiting atomic mobility. In contrast, if the synthesis is modified to allow even a modest degree of atomic rearrangement (e.g. via a mild annealing step) prior to quenching, the increased atomic mobility will promote local elemental segregation during service, leading to degradation of the desired structure and performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized by rapid, low-temperature reduction of single-source precursors (i.e. with limited free atom mobility during formation).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled mild annealing pre-treatment step (i.e. a brief heating hold before rapid quenching) during synthesis to allow partial atomic diffusion, and compare these nanoparticles to a control batch prepared entirely by rapid low‐temperature synthesis.
generation.conditions: Both batches are subjected to service conditions relevant for catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric operation (473–1923 K) under identical atmospheres. The synthesis is otherwise identical (composition, precursor, and support), except for the controlled annealing step.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of atomic mixing/homogeneity in the nanoparticle lattice (i.e. the absence or presence of local elemental segregation).
generation.mechanism: Rapid low-temperature synthesis kinetically freezes the high-entropy, disordered solid solution by limiting atomic mobility; this suppresses diffusion-driven segregation even at high temperatures. Allowing a mild annealing step increases atomic mobility during formation, promoting early-stage elemental redistribution that leads to phase instability upon subsequent service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline control (rapid synthesis without annealing), nanoparticles produced with the pre-annealing intervention will show evidence (via XRD, TEM-EDX, or atom probe tomography) of emergent elemental segregation or phase separation after exposure to high-temperature service conditions, accompanied by degraded catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized by rapid low-temperature reduction (no pre-annealing), which are expected to maintain their single-phase, chemically homogeneous structure under high-temperature operation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to multi-element HEA nanoparticles prepared from solid, mixed precursors via low-temperature methods in systems where the mobility of the reduced metal atoms is limited. Service conditions are those specified (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics) and the evaluation is based on standard structural and performance metrics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold of atomic mobility (or annealing temperature/time) required to trigger appreciable segregation is uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy system and precursor chemistry. Quantitative differences in measured properties are therefore not predicted precisely without further empirical calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles using the same single-source precursor and support. One batch is synthesized by rapid low-temperature reduction (control) while the other undergoes a predetermined mild annealing step before quenching. Subject both batches to accelerated thermal aging at 773–1173 K for a designated period. Characterize the structural homogeneity (using X-ray diffraction, high-resolution TEM with EDX mapping, or atom probe tomography) and test catalytic/thermoelectric performance before and after thermal treatment.
measurements: Elemental distribution homogeneity (TEM-EDX mapping or atom probe tomography)
Catalytic reaction rates or thermoelectric figure-of-merit performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles produced with the controlled mild annealing step do not show statistically significant differences (e.g., evidence of elemental segregation or phase separation) or degraded performance compared to the control after high-temperature exposure, then the hypothesis that limited atomic mobility is necessary to preserve the high-entropy state is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. The proposed formation principle is supported by simulations of the nanoparticle formation

Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. Extending this to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can provide a way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nano

Further in situ annealing studies up to 1173 K also confirms the excellent thermal stability of nanoparticles. We believe the mechanistic details reported in this work would not only guide the nanoparticles synthesis through Joule heating-based methods, but also pave the way on understanding other rapid high temperature synthesis approaches.
